objectives: At the completion of this course, students will be able to identify and explain the epistemological assumptions underlying interpretivist approaches to qualitative inquiry.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to distinguish among various qualitative research methodologies, including ethnography, narrative inquiry, arts-based, and archival methods.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to design a qualitative research study, aligning research questions, methodology, and methods.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to conduct effective qualitative data generation and collection through interviews, observations, and document analysis.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to apply coding techniques to qualitative data to generate patterns and themes.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to critically evaluate the rigor and trustworthiness of qualitative research studies.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to demonstrate reflexivity and address ethical considerations in qualitative research design and practice.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to communicate qualitative research findings clearly and persuasively in both written and oral formats.
topics: Introduction to interpretivist qualitative inquiry: Epistemological assumptions 2.
Sampling and recruitment 3.
Research design in qualitative studies: Developing research questions and aligning methods 4.
Overview of qualitative methodologies: Ethnography, narrative inquiry, art-based inquiry and archival methods 5.
Data collection methods including (a) conducting interviews and focus groups;
(b) observations and fieldwork techniques;
(c) document and archival analysis 6.
Coding and data analysis including (a) introduction to coding and thematic analysis;
(b) advanced coding techniques and use of software tools 7.
Quality in qualitative research 8.
Reflexivity and the role of the researcher: Ethics and positionality 9.
Writing qualitative research: Strategies for reporting findings 10.
Critiquing qualitative research: Evaluating published studies

objectives: By the end of the course, students will learn to articulate the historical and theoretical foundations of critical participatory inquiry (CPI).
By the end of the course, students will learn to describe the common characteristics of CPI.
By the end of the course, students will learn to discuss common practices associated with designing CPI studies.
By the end of the course, students will learn to outline ethical considerations common to the CPI process.
By the end of the course, students will learn to describe the various types of data collected in CPI studies.
By the end of the course, students will learn to design a CPI study.
By the end of the course, students will learn to carry out participatory/collaborative fieldwork, including multiple forms of data collection.
By the end of the course, students will learn to carry out participatory/collaborative data analysis.

objectives: Students will be able to detail the variety of ways knowledge and science have been conceptualized through history and across disciplines.
Students will be able to explore divergent, conflicting, and new paths in knowledge generation and translation, and consider where and how these may evolve in the future.
Students will be able to articulate the contributions historically marginalized people have made to the nature of knowledge in general and science specifically.
Students will be able to identify the nature of philosophical problems and solutions in social science research.
Students will be able to describe the ways in which different philosophical approaches to science inform research design.
Students will be able to participate in dialogue with others and develop the capacity to be more reflective in their own work.
Students will be able to identify and share new possibilities for their own research and strengthen scholarly writing skills.
topics: The History of the Disciplines in the Social Sciences The Role of History The Language and Role of Philosophy Normal Sci

objectives: Students will be able to produce a data inventory that includes research questions and data appropriate for a qualitative or mixed methods research design.
Students will be able to explain how analysis is informed by theory.

Students will be able to apply a range of analytic approaches to interpret qualitative data.

Students will be able to reflect on ethical issues as these relate to different analytical approaches.

objectives: As a student, you will become familiar with the aims, assumptions and methods of various approaches to ethnographic research;
As a student, you will gain experience in carrying out the major phases of ethnographic research;
As a student, you will design, gain access to the field, engage in data collection, data analysis and writing up the final report;
As a student, you will understand the role of theory in ethnographic research;
As a student, you will understand your own subjectivities in relation to your fieldwork;
As a student, you will use established codes of ethics to consider ethical issues that may occur in ethnographic research;
As a student, you will be able to assess the quality of ethnographic research.

objectives: By the end of this course, students should be able to identify key principles of culturally responsive program evaluation.
By the end of this course, students should be able to investigate theoretical possibilities and various ways of applying culturally responsive program evaluation strategies in different contexts.
By the end of this course, students should be able to reflect on the personal and conceptual presuppositions and assumptions one brings to program evaluation.

By the end of this course, students should be able to reflect on key challenges and issues encountered in the field.
